title: 1 Samuel 7:15–17
context: The chapter closes with Samuel’s ordinary work. He judged Israel all the days of his life. Year by year he went in a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and he judged Israel in all those places. His return was to Ramah, for his house was there; he judged Israel there, and he built an altar to the LORD there. Both traditions read the unit as the picture of a lifelong judgeship: a circuit among named towns and a home with an altar at Ramah, spelled as the WEB spells them. This is the narrator’s account of Samuel’s settled ministry after the repentance and the help of the preceding verses. How an altar at Ramah sits alongside the larger question of a central place of worship is a discussion for other texts; it should not be forced into a contrast here, and the verse itself simply reports that he built an altar to the LORD at his home.

verses.text: Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.” The office is lifelong, and the notice matches the “all the days of Samuel” already named in verse 13.

Arminian readers hear a real, continuing stewardship. He judges Israel not only in the crisis at Mizpah but for the whole of his life; the help of Ebenezer is followed by lasting labor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the narrator’s summary of Samuel’s life work. The same span in which the LORD’s hand was against the Philistines is the span of this judgeship.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: a faithful, lifelong judging of Israel, not a brief emergency role.

verses.text: He went from year to year in a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah; and he judged Israel in all those places.
verses.arminianNotes:
He went from year to year in a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah; and he judged Israel in all those places. The work is regular and local, among three towns the WEB names without hyphen or variant spelling.

Arminian readers hear a practiced, yearly round. He actually goes, and he judges in all those places, not only at home. The people can find a judge in the circuit as well as in the crisis.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same circuit as the ordinary means of this judgeship. Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah are already heavy with Israel’s memory; here they are simply the places of Samuel’s yearly judgment.

Both traditions take the verse as the map of his public work, shared ground, without inventing a contrast over why these three towns are named.

verses.text: His return was to Ramah, for his house was there, and he judged Israel there; and he built an altar to the LORD there.
verses.arminianNotes:
His return was to Ramah, for his house was there, and he judged Israel there; and he built an altar to the LORD there. Home, judgment, and an altar are joined at Ramah.

Arminian readers hear a life rooted in a place. He returns to Ramah because his house is there; he judges there as well as on the circuit; and he builds an altar to the LORD there, a fact the verse states without explaining further.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take Ramah as house, court, and altar. The altar is built to the LORD; how that reports sits with other texts about a central sanctuary is a larger question, and it is not a settled consensus or an Arminian–Reformed fork in this verse.

Both traditions read the close as Samuel’s home ministry under the LORD, shared ground after Ebenezer, and the last word of the chapter.
